item.title: Episode 10: Portfolio Management, Part 1
item.itunes:title: Episode 10: Portfolio Management, Part 1
item.description:
Portfolio Management, Part 1 (Section II.B, 9% of the exam): tax-aware investing. The first Portfolio Management episode. Middle-pace driving edition with a one-minute opening recap and a 30-second preview of Part 2.
Covered (KS 1–3, 9): tax efficiency (Defer, Character, Location, Losses); ranking the tax-friendliness of assets, vehicles and accounts; taxable-equivalent yield; tax drag on future value; tax-loss harvesting (Find, Sell, Swap, Wait, Record), choosing candidates, direct indexing and gain harvesting; judging managers after tax (Turnover, Timing, Type, Tax-cost) with worked after-tax return calculations for equity and bond managers; portfolio construction strategies, implementation, vehicles (ETFs, SMAs, UMAs, private funds, insurance wrappers), lot selection and charitable gifts of stock; asset location with an example; and tax-smart spending order.
Also: Exam Traps, a short case ("Preston's Shelf"), and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. Return examples are illustrations. Memory tricks are just ours. Cheat sheet: ep10-cheatsheet.pdf.
All characters and firms are fictional.

item.title: Episode 9: Tax Planning, Part 4
item.itunes:title: Episode 9: Tax Planning, Part 4
item.description:
Tax Planning, Part 4 (Section II.A, 15% of the exam): options, exchanges, insurance and retirement. The last tax episode. Middle-pace driving edition with a one-minute opening recap and a 30-second preview of Portfolio Management.
Covered (KS 13, 14, 17–20): NQSOs and ISOs (Grant, Exercise, Sell, Spread), holding periods, basis, the $100,000 rule, disqualifying dispositions, AMT, a worked example and exercise strategies, plus 83(b); like-kind exchanges (Real Quick, Forty-five, One-eighty) and boot; qualified small business stock (Corporate Original Small Active) with the post-July 4, 2025 tiered exclusion and $15M cap, §1045 rollovers, and the risks and benefits of each; how life insurance, MECs, annuities, disability and LTC are taxed; the three tax buckets, Roth vs. traditional, the 2026 plan limits, multiple plans, cash balance plans, solo 401(k) vs. SEP, HSAs, 529 updates, coordination strategies, distributions and inherited accounts.
Also: Exam Traps, a short case ("Mateo's Startup"), and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. Figures are for 2026. Memory tricks are just ours. Cheat sheet: ep09-cheatsheet.pdf.
All characters and firms are fictional.

item.title: Episode 8: Tax Planning, Part 3
item.itunes:title: Episode 8: Tax Planning, Part 3
item.description:
Tax Planning, Part 3 (Section II.A, 15% of the exam): trusts, high-net-worth issues and pass-throughs. Middle-pace driving edition. It opens with a one-minute "where we are" recap and closes with a 30-second preview of Part 4.
Covered (KS 2–4, 15–16): the three trust tax regimes (grantor, non-grantor, tax-exempt CRT), compressed 2026 trust brackets, DNI, simple vs. complex trusts and the 65-day rule; grantor trusts and the IDGT; a tour of every trust type on the outline (revocable, GRAT, GRUT, GRIT, irrevocable, credit shelter, marital/QTIP, ILIT, spendthrift, self-settled, DAPT, dynasty/GST, CRT, CLT); high-net-worth tax issues (Never Ask Grandma Silly Questions); intrafamily income shifting and the kiddie tax (Grandkids Kindly Fund Every Investment); pass-through entities and how income keeps its character; the QBI deduction; the four loss gates (Big Ants Prefer Excess); passive-loss limits, the $25,000 rental allowance, carryforwards and dispositions.
Also: Exam Traps, a short case ("The Montalvo Rentals"), and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. Figures are for tax year 2026. Memory tricks are just ours. Cheat sheet: ep08-cheatsheet.pdf.
All characters and firms are fictional.

item.itunes:title: Episode 6: Tax Planning, Part 1
item.description:

item.title: Episode 5: Family Dynamics, Part 2
item.itunes:title: Episode 5: Family Dynamics, Part 2
item.description:
Section 3: Family Dynamics, Part 2 (extra-slow edition, made for listening while driving). Family Dynamics is 9% of the CPWA exam, within Human Dynamics (18%). It opens with a one-minute "where we are" recap and closes with a 30-second preview of Tax Planning. Lists are counted, taken one item at a time and repeated slowly, with longer pauses, three mini recaps and four quiz breaks.
Covered (KS 4–7): human, social and financial capital (Me, We, and Money) and the family education plan; the elements of a successful family meeting (Before, during, after); governance structures (A Council Can Build Committees), the family employment policy, and matching governance to the ownership stage (controlling owner, sibling partnership, cousin consortium); the family mission statement (the five W's and one H) vs. the family constitution; the seven-step financial planning process (Ugly Iguanas Always Dance Poorly In Miami) and its five implementation steps (A Plan Should Come Complete); communicating across generations (three T's and two L's); navigating family conflict, including mediation vs. arbitration and which specialists to bring in; and tools for generational change (Some Elders Gracefully Exit, Passing Power).
Also: Exam Traps, a short case ("The Montalvo Succession"), and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. A one-page cheat sheet goes with this episode.
Next: Tax Planning begins with Episode 6.
All characters and firms are fictional. Memory tricks are study aids, not official terms.

item.description:
Section 3: Family Dynamics, Part 1 (extra-slow edition, made for listening while driving). Family Dynamics is 9% of the CPWA exam, within Human Dynamics (18%). Covered (KS 1–3): client discovery (goals, challenges, opportunities); the six question areas and six document groups for a family profile (memory trick: Before Every Family Interview, Take Minutes); immigrants vs. natives to wealth; the seven common characteristics of high-net-worth families (the seven P's) and fair vs. equal; what a family office does; single-family vs. multi-family office, plus virtual, embedded and hybrid models; choosing the best-fit infrastructure by wealth level and objectives; and family roles in trusts, closely held businesses (the three-circle model), family foundations, LLCs and charities (The Big Family Loves Charity).

item.title: Episode 3: Behavioral Finance, Part 2
item.itunes:title: Episode 3: Behavioral Finance, Part 2
item.description:
Section 2: Behavioral Finance & Investor Psychology, Part 2 (slow edition, made for listening while driving). The section is 6% of the CPWA exam, within Human Dynamics (18%). It opens with a two-minute warm-up quiz on Episode 2, then goes through the rest of the learning objectives at a calmer pace, with counted lists, pauses, three mini recaps and four quiz breaks.
Covered: what makes a bias emotional; the seven emotional biases (memory trick: LOSS ERA) and the four pairs the exam likes to contrast; educate vs. accommodate (Pompian's "moderate vs. adapt"): the two guidelines, the four boxes, education and accommodation tools, the best practical allocation, and a three-question exam routine (Name it, sort it, size it); the four behavioral investor types (Please Follow Investment Advice: Preserver, Follower, Independent, Accumulator), how to diagnose them, "emotional bookends, cognitive middle," and how each type reacts to the same market move; generations (Silent through Gen Z, "Depression Babies," Boomers vs. Millennials); and earned vs. inherited wealth.
Also: Exam Traps, the short case "The Two Portfolios," and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. A one-page cheat sheet goes with this episode.
Next: Family Dynamics, Part 1.
All characters and firms are fictional.

Covered: what makes a bias emotional; the seven emotional biases (memory trick: LOSS ERA) and the four pairs the exam likes to contrast; educate vs. accommodate (Pompian's "moderate vs. adapt"): the two guidelines, the four boxes, education and accommodation tools, the best practical allocation, and a three-question exam routine (Name it, sort it, size it); the four behavioral investor types (Please Follow Investment Advice: Preserver, Follower, Independent, Accumulator), how to diagnose them, "emotional bookends, cognitive middle," and how each type reacts to the same market move; generations (Silent through Gen Z, "Depression Babies," Boomers vs. Millennials); and earned vs. inherited wealth.
Also: Exam Traps, the short case "The Two Portfolios," and the exam must-knows with Doña Pilar. A one-page cheat sheet goes with this episode.

item.itunes:title: Episode 1: Ethics (The Pilot)
item.description:
Module: Overview & Ethics. Three case files and one question that sounds simple and never is: who, exactly, is my client?
The Case of the Three Wedding Rings: Don Octavio, a US citizen who died in Colombia, a widow without a US passport, and a lawyer who arrives much too early with papers to sign. Covers worldwide estate tax, the QDOT and conflicts of interest. The Case of the Silent Trust: the Castañedas, a Delaware dynasty trust, and a son who starts asking questions. Covers confidentiality and preparing heirs. The Case of the Sixty-Thousand-Dollar Teacup: tea with Doña Pilar and US estate tax for nonresident non-citizens.
The IWI Code of Professional Responsibility runs through all three, followed by Teo's Pop Quiz, Fabi's Call and a Lightning Recap with Doña Pilar.
All characters, families, firms and banks are fictional.

item.description:
Welcome to the Casebook, Fabi. Meet your host Margo (a senior wealth strategist, CPWA and part-time detective) and Teo (a junior associate, quiz master and proud owner of a buzzer), and find out how every episode works: Cold Open, the Huddle, the Case Room, the Real-World File, Teo's Pop Quiz, Fabi's Call and the Lightning Recap. The whole thing fits your commute.
Then meet the recurring cast you'll follow through the course: Don Octavio Salcedo and his box of home videos ("the Octavio Archive"), the widow Valentina, the young heiress Sofía, Rodrigo the in-law with a crypto hotel in Tulum, the family lawyer Dr. Villalba, the Castañedas of Guatemala City, the Montalvos of Lima, Preston Hale the private banker, Kendra from Growth, and Doña Pilar, who will ask the same question five times (on purpose).
All characters, families, firms and banks are fictional.
